_notes: Shared religious life: the diocesan seminarians from the studium's lectures, who become the diocese's priests. E3 §3.13. Hangs on dcm:met and the yearly dcm:* flags.

events.title: The Men From the Diocese
events.body: The first lecture of the theology years, and the back rows are the diocesan seminary's men, in clerical shirts, who have been sent across the city to the same hall since the diocese cannot staff a faculty and the order can, and {@diocesan_classmate} has sat beside you on purpose, since, he says, he wanted to see what a friar writes in the margins.

choices.label: Show him the margins
choices.outcome: They are mostly questions, and he laughs, and writes better ones in his, and the two of you argue in the margins for four years, and it is the friendship with the diocese that the order did not plan and you keep for life.

choices.label: Ask him what a diocesan seminarian writes
choices.outcome: He says: the bishop's name, and what the bishop would think, and it is a joke and is not, and it is the first thing you learn about the diocese from inside it, and you learn the rest from him over four years.

choices.label: Sit with the friars, as the friars do
choices.outcome: The friars sit in the middle and the diocesans at the back and the lecture is the same for both, and the man who wanted to see the margins sits with someone else, and the four years are the order's and not the diocese's, which is the usual thing, and is a loss.

events.title: He Envies the House
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} has come to supper at the house, since the friars may have guests on Thursdays, and has sat through the table and the recreation and Compline in the dark, and has said at the door, in a voice he did not mean to use, that the diocesan seminary has a dining hall and a chapel and nothing that was this, and that he did not know until tonight what he would not have.

choices.label: Say he may come any Thursday
choices.outcome: He comes most Thursdays for four years and is the diocese's man who knows a house, and is a pastor who builds a table in his rectory, and says at your jubilee that it was the Thursdays, and it was, and the order never knew it gave them.

choices.label: Tell him what the table costs, since he has seen only the supper
choices.outcome: He listens and says he would pay it, and does not enter, since he is the diocese's, and it is the honest exchange the two institutions rarely have, and it is between the two of you, and holds.

choices.label: Say goodnight, and let him carry it
choices.outcome: He carries it. He is a lonely priest in a lonely diocese for a decade and then is not, since he finds two others, and says he learned it from a supper he was not invited back to, which is true and is a little on you.

events.title: He Asks About the Order
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} has asked, on the walk from the hall, whether a seminarian of the diocese can enter the order, and how, and whether the friars would take a man the bishop has paid four years of tuition for, and he is serious, and it is the fourth year, and the bishop has a claim, and so, in a way, do you.

choices.label: Tell him how, and that it would cost the diocese and him both
choices.outcome: He goes to the vocation director and then to his bishop, who is not glad and lets him go, and he is a novice a year after you are ordained, and a friar of the province, and the diocese does not forget who talked to him on a walk.

choices.label: Tell him to be ordained for the diocese first, and see
choices.outcome: He is ordained for the diocese and is a good priest of it and comes to supper on Thursdays for thirty years, and does not enter, and says he would have and is glad he did not, and both are true, and it was the walk.

choices.label: Say the order is not what he thinks from Thursdays
choices.outcome: He is quiet and says he had suspected it, and stays where he is, and is a pastor, and the two of you have the argument about the two lives at every jubilee, and neither wins, and it is the best argument you have.

events.title: The Same June
events.body: The diocese ordains in June and so does the order, and this year the two are a week apart in the same cathedral, and {@diocesan_classmate} is prostrate on the same stone seven days after you, and has asked you to vest him, which a diocesan man asks his father or his pastor, and he has asked a friar.

choices.label: Vest him
choices.outcome: You vest him. The bishop, who notices things, notices a friar's hands on a diocesan chasuble and says nothing, and the man's mother says the friar was the one, and the two of you have the same June for the rest of your lives, and count from it.

choices.label: Tell him his pastor should, and stand in the second row
choices.outcome: His pastor vests him and is moved to be asked, and you are in the second row, and he finds you there, and it was the right row, and the pastor is the diocese's man for him for a decade, which he needed more than a friar.

choices.label: Vest him with his pastor, one on each side
choices.outcome: The rubrics have no view. The bishop raises an eyebrow. The man has a friar and a pastor at his ordination and a diocese and an order at his back, and it is the picture on his wall for forty years, and the order is in it.

events.title: His First Parish
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} has been a curate for a year in a parish across the diocese and has telephoned to say the pastor is impossible and the parish is dying and would you come and see, and preach the Sunday, since the pastor has said a friar may, and it would be a favour and a look at the diocese from the inside.

choices.label: Go, and preach it
choices.outcome: The parish is dying and the pastor is impossible and the homily is four minutes on one thing, and the man says afterward that the parish will talk about it for a year, and it does, and the pastor asks the prior for the friar again, which is the beginning of the asks.

choices.label: Go, and listen to him for an evening instead
choices.outcome: It is an evening of the diocese from a curate's chair, and it is what he needed, and you learn what a diocesan first year costs, which a friar does not otherwise know, and he is easier for a year, and the parish is what it was.

choices.label: Say the prior would have to be asked, and ask him
choices.outcome: The prior says yes, since it is a Sunday, and the man learns the road, and the pastor learns it too, and writes to the prior himself the next time, which is how it should go, and the homily is good.

events.title: A Classmate for a Neighbour
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} is a pastor now, and his parish is in this diocese, and he has come to the house to say so and to say, at the table, that he would like the two parishes to do something together, since the diocese and the order do not, and he has a Lenten idea and a Corpus Christi one and the friars are looking at you.

choices.label: Say yes to both
choices.outcome: The Lenten thing is a shared mission and the Corpus Christi thing is a procession from his church to yours, and the diocese notices that a diocesan parish and an order's parish walked the same street behind the same monstrance, and the bishop mentions it, and the prior is pleased and says so.

choices.label: Say yes to the procession and not the mission
choices.outcome: The procession is the thing anyway. The two parishes walk the street once a year for twenty years, and the mission is preached by someone else, and the man says the friars gave the diocese a feast, and it is enough.

choices.label: Say the prior will answer, and let the house decide
choices.outcome: The prior says yes to one and the house grumbles about the other, and the man learns how the house decides, and is patient, and the procession happens, and it is the house's thing then and not yours, which was right.

events.title: He Reads Your File
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} is at the chancery now, a monsignor, and it is the vicar for clergy's desk, and he has telephoned to say, off the record, that the bishop's office keeps a file on the friars in the diocese as it does on its own men, and that yours is on his desk, and that there is a thing in it he would like to ask you about before the bishop does.

choices.label: Ask him what the thing is, and answer it
choices.outcome: It is a thing you said from a pulpit, reported by someone, and you tell him what you said and why, and he writes a note in the file that says so, and the bishop reads the note and not the report, and the friar has a friend at the chancery, which the province could not have arranged.

choices.label: Say the file is the province's business and the provincial's to answer
choices.outcome: He says the provincial does not sit in this chancery and that he does, and is hurt, and puts the report in the file without a note, and the bishop reads the report, and it is a season before it is mended.

choices.label: Thank him, and ask what else is in it
choices.outcome: He tells you, which he should not, and it is the diocese's view of a friar over fifteen years, and it is fairer than you had feared and colder than you had hoped, and you know what the bishop knows, which is worth a great deal.

events.title: The Classmate Is a Bishop
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate}, who sat beside you in the theology years and asked what a friar writes in the margins, is to be a bishop, of a diocese two states away, and has telephoned before the announcement, which he should not have, to say so, and to ask whether you would come to the consecration and sit with his family, since his family does not know a bishop and knows you.

choices.label: Go, and sit with the family
choices.outcome: You sit with the mother, who remembers the vesting or the Thursdays, and the new bishop finds you from the sanctuary, and the order has a friend in a mitre two states away, which is a thing provinces pray for and cannot arrange, and he writes at Christmas for the rest of his life.

choices.label: Send a letter, and the founder's word
choices.outcome: He reads it at the lunch, to the table, and the table does not understand it, and he does, and it is the thing he has on his desk for a reign, and he is a better bishop for a friar's word than for the chancery's, and says so, once, to the nuncio.

choices.label: Say the house cannot spare you for a weekend two states away
choices.outcome: He understands, since he knows the house, and is a little hurt, and the friendship is Christmas cards after that, and the province has a bishop it might have had a friend in, and did not, quite.

events.title: He Has Left
events.body: {@closest_diocesan_classmate} has left the priesthood, and the diocese has done what dioceses do, which is to say nothing, and he has written to you, since a friar is not the diocese, to say he is well and married and teaching and that he would like to come to supper, once, since the house was the thing he missed, and the prior has said it is your guest.

choices.label: Have him to supper, and walk the cloister after
choices.outcome: The house does what it does with him, and the cloister is an hour and thirty years, and he says he does not regret it and has missed it every day, and you say the same in reverse, and both are true, and he sends a card at Christmas, and the house keeps the card.

choices.label: Write back, and say supper another year
choices.outcome: Another year is three, and then he comes, and it is the same supper later, and he says he had needed it sooner, and you had known, and the prior had said it was your guest, and it was on you.

choices.label: Ask the diocese's man, his old pastor, to come too
choices.outcome: The old pastor comes, unsure, and the three of you sit at the table, and the diocese and the order and the world eat together for an evening, and the old pastor says on the step that he had not known how to do this, and now does, and does it for the next one.

events.title: The Classmate's Funeral
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} has died, a pastor, of the thing that takes pastors at sixty, and the diocese is burying him from his own church, and the bishop is to preach, and the family has asked, through the vicar for clergy, whether the friar who sat beside him in the theology years would say a word after Communion, since he had asked for it, in a paper the chancellor found.

choices.label: Say the word: what he wrote in the margins, and what it became
choices.outcome: The church is quiet and then not, and the bishop, who preached first, says afterward that he had not known the man, which is true and is a thing bishops learn at funerals, and the diocese hears a friar say what its priest was, and remembers both.

choices.label: Say three sentences, and sit down
choices.outcome: They are the right three, and the family says so, and the bishop says the friar knew when to stop, which from a bishop is a great deal, and the deanery remembers the three sentences longer than the homily.

choices.label: Decline; the bishop preached, and it is the diocese's funeral
choices.outcome: The family is hurt and the bishop is not, and the chancellor puts the paper back in the file, and you sit in the nave with the people, and it was his funeral and you were at it, and the word was not said, and you say it at his grave, alone.

events.title: The Chancery Corridor
events.body: The bishop's office has asked the friars for something, and you are the one sent, and the corridor of the chancery has {@diocesan_classmate} in it, a monsignor now, who has stopped and said that he had heard the friars were coming and had hoped it was you, and that the bishop's office will say no to the thing, and that he could make it yes, if the friars would do something for the diocese first.

choices.label: Ask what the something is, and take it back to the prior
choices.outcome: It is a Sunday supply for a parish the diocese cannot staff, for a year, and the prior says yes, since it is a year, and the bishop's office says yes to the thing, and the diocese and the order have done a trade in a corridor, which is how dioceses and orders do most things, and both are the better for it.

choices.label: Say the friars do not trade, and let the office say no
choices.outcome: The office says no. The man shrugs and says the friars never did, and the thing is not done, and the prior says you were right and that he would have traded, and the diocese thinks the friars are proud, which they are, a little.

choices.label: Ask him, as a friend, to make it yes without the something
choices.outcome: He does, since it is you, and the office says yes, and he has spent something of his own at the chancery for a friar, and says so, once, and you owe him, and pay it in ten years when he needs a friar, and it is the friendship the theology years were for.

events.title: The Same Deanery
events.body: {@diocesan_classmate} is a pastor in the deanery now, and the meeting has two men in it who sat in the same lecture hall twenty years ago, one in a habit and one in a shirt, and the dean has said, not quite as a joke, that the deanery has a faction, and {@deanery_priest} has said that at least it is a faction that knows its theology.

choices.label: Be the faction: the two of you, on the things the deanery gets wrong
choices.outcome: The deanery gets fewer things wrong for a decade and resents it a little and is grateful more, and the dean says the two of you should be on every committee and are, and the bishop's office hears that the friars and the diocese can work together, from a deanery.

choices.label: Sit apart, and let the deanery see two men and not a pair
choices.outcome: The deanery sees two men, and they are both good, and the friendship is at the lunch and not the meeting, and the dean says the two of you were careful, and you were, and it was right and a little cold.

choices.label: Say the faction meets on Thursdays and the dean is welcome
choices.outcome: The dean comes on a Thursday, to the house, and sees the table, and the deanery has a dean who knows a house, and it changes how the deanery treats the friars for the rest of his time, and the man from the lectures says it was the Thursdays again.

events.title: Two Jubilees
events.body: Twenty-five years, and the diocese's jubilee Mass is the same week as the order's, and {@diocesan_classmate} has proposed, since the two of you were ordained a week apart, that the two jubilees be one: the bishop's cathedral, the order's friars in the choir, the diocese's priests in the nave, and two men at the altar who sat in the same hall.

choices.label: Say yes, and take it to the prior and the bishop's office together
choices.outcome: Both say yes, since neither had thought of it, and it is the Mass the diocese talks about for a decade: a friar and a diocesan pastor concelebrating a jubilee, the bishop presiding, the province in the choir, and the man from the lectures preaching four minutes on what a friar writes in the margins.

choices.label: Say the order's is the house's, and come to his
choices.outcome: You go to his and he to yours, a week apart, and each preaches at the other's, and it is two Masses and one friendship, and the diocese and the order see each other's jubilee, which they had not, and the bishop says at the second that he had been at the first.

choices.label: Say the house's jubilee is the house's, and send a letter to his
choices.outcome: He reads the letter at his lunch, and it is the founder's word or the order's, and the diocese hears it, and you are at the house's Mass and not at his, and he understands, and it is a week you think about.
